Both score 60. Tie-break: Example B has a promised_at and A does not, so B ranks above A.
6) Status changes (state machine)
FROM
TO
RULE
received
preparing
Allowed
received
cancelled
Allowed
preparing
ready
Allowed
ready
picked_up
Allowed
anything else
anything else
Rejected
picked_up and cancelled are terminal. No order can skip a step ( received cannot jump to 
ready ). Repeating the same transition (e.g. acknowledging an already preparing order) is 
an error, not a silent success.
Enforce this on the server, hiding a button in the UI is not enough. If someone calls the API 
directly, the server must reject an illegal transition with a clear error.
7) API
METHOD
PATH
BEHAVIOR
GET
/orders/queue
Default: received and preparing , sorted by score. Optional query param 
status=received or status=preparing to filter. Each order in the 
response includes its computed score .
4/9


--- page 5 ---
POST
/orders/:id/start
Transition: received → preparing .
POST
/orders/:id/ready
Transition: preparing → ready .
POST
/orders/:id/pickup
Transition: ready → picked_up .
POST
/orders/:id/cancel
Transition: received → cancelled .
For illegal transitions or other validation errors, return a 4xx response with a stable, machine-
readable error code (e.g. INVALID_TRANSITION , ORDER_NOT_FOUND ). Choose your codes and 
document them briefly in the README.
8) UI
One page: the Kitchen Display.
• A table showing the active queue: score, customer name, order type, items summary, wait 
time, promised time, VIP badge, status;
• A way to filter by received , preparing , or the default active queue;
• Actions to advance each order to its next status. Only show the action that is valid for the 
current status;
• A way to cancel a received order;
• An empty state when the queue has no orders;
• When the API rejects a transition, the error must be visible on the screen (not just in the 
browser console);
Use MUI. Match the layout to a dense internal tool (think ops dashboard), not a marketing 
page.
The score and the sort order must come from the API. The UI must not contain a second copy 
of the scoring formula. The table displays whatever the API returns, in the order the API 
returns it.
9) Technical constraints
One repository, wwo apps (API and web). Do not depend on any private or external repository.
9.1) API
• Node.js 22;
• JavaScript;
• Express;
• Sequelize 6, with migrations (do not rely on sync() for schema creation);
• PostgreSQL 16;
• Jest;
5/9


--- page 6 ---
Organize the API in layers:
LAYER
RESPONSIBILITY
Endpoint
HTTP only. Read the request, call the module, write the response. Thin.
Module
Business logic: priority scoring, state machine transitions.
Repository
Data access: Sequelize queries, includes, filters.
Schema
Sequelize models and migrations.
The priority function must be pure. It receives the order data and now as arguments, and 
returns a number. Its Jest tests run without PostgreSQL and without mocking Sequelize.
9.2) Web
• Vite;
• React 19;
• TypeScript;
• MUI 7;
• Vitest (for extra points only; see below);
9.3) Database
Ship a docker-compose.yml that starts PostgreSQL 16 only. Use host port 5433 so a local 
Postgres on 5432 does not collide.
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: kitchen_queue
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: kitchen_queue
      POSTGRES_DB: kitchen_queue
    ports:
      - "5433:5432"
9.4) Getting started
From a clean machine, the README should guide someone through:
1. docker compose up -d (start Postgres)
2.One install command
3.One db:setup command (runs migrations + seed)
4.One dev command (starts both the API and the web app)
Suggested ports: API on 4000 , web on 5173 .
6/9


--- page 7 ---
9.5) Seed
You write the seed, it must contain menu items and orders with order items.
Seed dates must be relative to the UTC time when the seed runs (e.g. "placed 2 hours ago", 
"promised in 20 minutes"). Hard-coded calendar dates go stale and break the demo.
Include enough rows to demonstrate:
• Every order type ( dine_in , takeout , delivery )
• At least one VIP and one non-VIP order
• A wait-time cap (an order old enough that wait-time points hit the maximum)
• A complexity cap (an order with enough total prep time to hit the maximum)
• A tie on score broken by promised_at
• Orders in different statuses ( received , preparing , and at least one ready that is not in 
the active queue)
Tests do not use the seed, they pass their own fixtures and a frozen now .
10) Tests (Required)
FRAMEWORK
WHAT IS PROVES
Jest (priority)
Score calculation, both caps (wait-time and complexity), all promised_at buckets (within 30 min, 
within 60 min, beyond, null), tie-break, and at least one case where a lower base-weight type wins on 
the rest of the formula (e.g. a delivery VIP with a tight promise beats a dine_in non-VIP).
Jest 
(transitions)
Every legal transition succeeds. Illegal transitions are rejected (skipping a step, repeating the same 
status, transitioning from a terminal status). A cancelled or picked-up order does not appear in the 
default queue.
Priority tests must freeze now . A test that calls Date.now() and hopes the clock still matches 
is a failing submission.
11) Extra points
Do these only after the required core is solid and you can fully explain it. Skipping all of them 
does not count against you. In DECISIONS.md , note which extras you attempted and which 
you left out.
11.1) POST /orders endpoint
API only, no UI form needed. Validate that items is non-empty, each menu_item_id 
references an existing menu item, and each quantity is a positive integer. Include at least 
one Jest test for a validation error.
7/9


--- page 8 ---
11.2) Vitest component test
The cancel button is only shown for received orders; or the queue table renders an empty 
state when there are no orders.
11.3) Playwright end-to-end
One happy path: the queue renders a seeded order, the expeditor starts preparation, and the 
status changes on screen. Wire it with Playwright's webServer config so npm run test:e2e 
boots what it needs.
12) What to submit
A git repository we can clone, with:
•
README.md — prerequisites (Docker, Node 22), the four commands to get running, ports, 
and your API error codes;
•
DECISIONS.md — the sections listed below;
• The API, the web app, migrations, seed, and tests;
12.1) DECISIONS.md sections
Write a few short paragraphs for each. We read these before the panel.
1.Scope
• What you built and what you cut because of the 4-hour box. Which extra points you 
attempted and which you skipped;
2.Layers
• What lives in the module, the repository, and the UI. Name one rule you refused to put 
in the UI and why;
3.Priority
• How the score is produced at request time, and one edge case that was easy to get 
wrong;
4.Transitions
• Where the state machine is enforced, and what happens when someone tries to start an 
order that is already preparing ;
5.AI
• One AI suggestion you kept and one you rejected or rewrote. Quote the idea and 
explain your reasoning;
6.Next
• If this had to run in a real kitchen next month, name the first two changes you would 
make. Do not implement them;
8/9


--- page 9 ---
13) The Interview
Plan on a short walkthrough of your DECISIONS.md and the priority rule, followed by a live 
change to this repository. The change will be a product tweak to ranking or status, in the area 
you already built. We will not ask you to re-architect the app, and we will not ask you to 
implement the extra-point items.
Arrive with Docker running and both apps able to boot in a couple of minutes. We would 
rather watch you change the code than watch you install dependencies.
14) Out of Scope
Authentication, user accounts, and roles. Payments or billing. A real customer entity (just a 
name string on the order). Pagination. A design-system package, Storybook, or CI pipeline. 
Restify, Redis, or background jobs. Real-time updates (WebSockets). Pixel-perfect visuals.
You may deviate from the suggested layout below. If you do, explain why in DECISIONS.md .
api/
  src/
web/
  src/
ai-logs/
docker-compose.yml
README.md
DECISIONS.md
9/9

content.text:
## 1. Hidden-content scan: the PDF is clean

I extracted the PDF with PyMuPDF in an isolated scratchpad venv and checked each text span:

- **White or near-white text, tiny fonts, off-page text, invisible render mode, transparency:** none found.
- **Zero-width or other unusual Unicode:** none found.
- **Annotations, links, embedded files, JavaScript, auto-run actions, hidden layers:** none found. The scan flagged 3 objects for an "auto-action" marker, but they were false alarms: the marker matched part of a font name (`AAAAAA+InterVariable`).
- **White-filled shapes:** these are table cell backgrounds from the export. No extracted text sits outside the visible content.
- **Metadata:** a normal Nuclino export from 2026-09-25 titled "Take-home test: Kitchen Display Queue."

There are no hidden instructions aimed at AI tools. Everything below comes from the visible text.

## 2. What they want

Build a Kitchen Display Queue: an Express/Sequelize/Postgres API plus a Vite/React 19/MUI 7 web app, with a 4-hour limit. They say directly what they grade:
- the business rules sit in the right layer
- ranking and status rules are easy to change, because in the interview you'll change them live
- you can explain every file
- you include an honest `DECISIONS.md` and the full AI chat logs in `ai-logs/`

**This conversation will go into `ai-logs/`, including this scan.** That's fine: checking an untrusted document before handing it to an AI is a reasonable step.

## 3. Plan

**Repo layout:** npm workspaces with `api/`, `web/`, `ai-logs/`, `docker-compose.yml` (Postgres 16 on host port 5433), `README.md` and `DECISIONS.md`. The root scripts are `npm install`, `npm run db:setup` (migrations + seed) and `npm run dev` (starts both apps with `concurrently`; API on 4000, web on 5173).

**API (JavaScript, layered as the spec asks):**
```
api/src/
  endpoints/orders.js        # HTTP only: parse request → call module → send response
  modules/priority.js        # pure: score(order, now); compareQueue(a, b)
  modules/priorityRules.js   # the weights and buckets as data → ranking changes are one-line edits
  modules/transitions.js     # the transition table + assertTransition(from, to); actions map start/ready/pickup/cancel to target statuses
  modules/orderService.js    # getQueue(filter, now), transition(id, action) — the repository is passed in
  repositories/orderRepository.js  # Sequelize queries/includes, conditional status update
  schema/models, migrations, seeders
  errors.js                  # AppError(code, httpStatus); one error-handling middleware
```
Key decisions to defend in the interview:
- **Status table as data:** a `{from: [to]}` table is the single source of truth, so a status change in the interview is one line.
- **Concurrency-safe transitions:** `UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND status = <expected from>`. If 0 rows update, return `INVALID_TRANSITION`. Two expeditors clicking at the same moment can't double-advance an order.
- **Score at request time:** fetch active orders with their items, score them in JS with `now` passed in, then sort. The API returns `score` (optionally the per-component breakdown, which helps with debugging and the walkthrough).
- **Error codes:** `ORDER_NOT_FOUND` (404), `INVALID_TRANSITION` (409), `INVALID_STATUS_FILTER` (400), `VALIDATION_ERROR` (400).

**Edge cases the spec leaves open (I'll pick a rule and document each):**
- A `promised_at` in the past (overdue) counts as "within 30 min" and scores 25 points.
- The gap between "30" and "31" minutes, e.g. 30m30s: I'll use `≤30 → 25` and `≤60 → 15` on exact seconds.
- Wait time uses whole minutes, floored. This is the "9m50s" trap they call out.
- Ties are broken by `promised_at` (nulls last), then `placed_at`, then `id`.

**Tests (Jest, frozen `now`, no database needed for the required tests):**
- **Priority:** worked examples A and B, both caps, all 4 promised-time buckets including the boundaries, every tie-break level, and the case where a delivery VIP beats a dine-in order.
- **Transitions:** every legal transition, skipping a step, repeating a status, and moving out of a terminal status. I'll also check that cancelled and picked-up orders don't appear in the queue, using `orderService` with an in-memory fake repository. That respects "no mocking Sequelize".

**Web (TypeScript, MUI 7):**
- one dense `KitchenDisplay` page with a table and the filter toggle (Active / Received / Preparing)
- a per-row next-action button, plus Cancel only on `received` orders
- an empty state and a visible error message when a transition fails
- no scoring logic in the UI; it renders rows in the order the API returns them
- the next-action labels come from a small map keyed by status, which is display-only

**Seed:** dates relative to now. It covers every order type, VIP and non-VIP, the wait-time cap, the complexity cap, a tie broken by `promised_at`, and orders in `received`, `preparing` and `ready`. I'll check that the seeded tie really produces equal scores.

**Extras, in order if there's time:** `POST /orders` with validation, then a Vitest test for the empty state and the cancel button, then Playwright.

**Finish:** README, `DECISIONS.md` (all 6 sections), export this session's transcript to `ai-logs/`, `git init` and commit, then a clean-start dry run of the 4 commands.

**Rough time:** scaffold and database ~45 min, modules and tests ~75 min, endpoints ~30 min, web ~60 min, docs and checks ~30 min.

## Before I start

1. **Extras:** should I do the core only, or add `POST /orders` and the Vitest test? I'd recommend both if the core finishes by about 3 hours, and skipping Playwright.
2. **Environment:** is Docker installed and running, and is Node 22 the active version (`node -v`)?
3. **Execution:** should I build everything end to end, or stop after each phase so you can review? I'd recommend stopping after each phase. You need to explain every file in the interview, so reviewing as we go will help a lot.

# Runs the API and the web app inside Node 22 containers, so the host needs only Docker.
# Postgres is NOT started here: start it first with `docker compose up -d` (docker-compose.yml).
# The containers reach it through the host port 5433.
name: kitchen-queue-app

services:
  api:
    image: node:22
    working_dir: /app
    # Every start: install deps, run migrations, re-seed (fresh relative dates), start the API.
    command: sh -c "npm install && npm run db:setup && npm run dev"
    restart: on-failure # retries if Postgres is not ready yet
    environment:
      DB_HOST: host.docker.internal
      DB_PORT: 5433
    extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"
    ports:
      - "4000:4000"
    volumes:
      - ./api:/app
      - api_node_modules:/app/node_modules

  web:
    image: node:22
    working_dir: /app
    command: sh -c "npm install && npm run dev"
    environment:
      API_URL: http://api:4000
    ports:
      - "5173:5173"
    volumes:
      - ./web:/app
      - web_node_modules:/app/node_modules
    depends_on:
      - api

volumes:
  api_node_modules:
  web_node_modules:

input.content:
# Kitchen Display Queue

An internal tool for a restaurant kitchen: the expeditor sees every active order ranked by a
priority score and moves each order through its preparation stages.

- **API**: Node.js 22, Express 5, Sequelize 6 (migrations), PostgreSQL 16, Jest — `api/`
- **Web**: Vite, React 19, TypeScript, MUI 7, Vitest, Playwright — `web/`

| Service    | Port |
| ---------- | ---- |
| API        | 4000 |
| Web        | 5173 |
| PostgreSQL | 5433 (host) → 5432 (container) |

## Getting started

Prerequisites: **Docker**. Node 22 is only needed for option B and for the Playwright e2e test.

### Option A — Docker only (no Node on the host)

```bash
docker compose up -d                              # 1. Postgres (docker-compose.yml)
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml up       # 2. API + web in Node 22 containers
```

The API container runs `npm install`, the migrations and the seed every time it starts, so each
start gives fresh demo data with dates relative to now. Open http://localhost:5173.

Run the unit tests inside the containers (while they are running):

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml exec api npm test
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml exec web npm test
```

### Option B — Node 22 on the host

```bash
docker compose up -d     # 1. start Postgres
npm install              # 2. installs the root, api/ and web/ dependencies
npm run db:setup         # 3. runs migrations + seed
npm run dev              # 4. starts the API and the web app
```

Do not run both options at the same time: they use the same ports.

## Tests

```bash
npm test                 # Jest (api) + Vitest (web); no database needed
```

- `api/tests/priority.test.js`: the scoring formula, both caps, every promised-time bucket, and the tie-break. All use a frozen `now`.
- `api/tests/transitions.test.js`: every legal and illegal status change, and the queue contents. Uses an in-memory repository.
- `api/tests/createOrder.test.js`: `POST /orders` validation.
- `web/src/components/QueueTable.test.tsx`: the empty state, and that Cancel appears only for received orders.

### End-to-end (Playwright, runs on the host)

```bash
docker compose up -d                          # Postgres must be running
npm install                                   # once
npx --prefix web playwright install chromium  # once
npm run test:e2e
```

If the apps are already running (from option A or B), Playwright reuses them. Otherwise it
re-seeds the database and starts them itself. If no `received` orders are left, run
`npm run db:setup` (or restart the API container) to reset the demo data.

## API

| Method | Path                  | Behavior |
| ------ | --------------------- | -------- |
| GET    | `/orders/queue`       | Active queue (`received` + `preparing`) sorted by score. `?status=received` or `?status=preparing` to filter. Each order includes `score`, `minutes_waiting` and `allowed_actions`. |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/start`   | `received` → `preparing` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/ready`   | `preparing` → `ready` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/pickup`  | `ready` → `picked_up` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/cancel`  | `received` → `cancelled` |
| POST   | `/orders`             | Create an order: `{ customer_name, type, is_vip?, promised_at?, items: [{ menu_item_id, quantity }] }` |

### Error codes

Every error response has the shape `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`.

| Code                    | HTTP | When |
| ----------------------- | ---- | ---- |
| `INVALID_TRANSITION`    | 409  | The status change is not allowed from the current status. This includes repeating a step, skipping a step, changing a terminal order, or losing a race with another request. |
| `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`       | 404  | No order with that id (or the id is not a positive integer). |
| `INVALID_STATUS_FILTER` | 400  | `status` query parameter is not `received` or `preparing`. |
| `VALIDATION_ERROR`      | 400  | `POST /orders` body is invalid, or a `menu_item_id` does not exist. |
| `INVALID_JSON`          | 400  | Request body is not valid JSON. |
| `ROUTE_NOT_FOUND`       | 404  | Unknown path. |
| `INTERNAL_ERROR`        | 500  | Unexpected server error (details are logged, not returned). |

## Project layout

```
api/src/
  endpoints/ordersEndpoint.js      HTTP only
  modules/priority.js              pure scoring + ranking (rules at the top of the file)
  modules/orderStatus.js           state machine (transition table)
  modules/orderValidation.js       POST /orders shape validation
  modules/orderModule.js           use cases: queue, status change, create
  repositories/orderRepository.js  Sequelize queries
  schema/                          models, migration, seed, DB config
web/src/
  components/KitchenDisplay.tsx    page: filter, data loading, error message
  components/QueueTable.tsx        the table
  api.ts                           fetch wrapper
web/e2e/                           Playwright test
ai-logs/                           AI conversation exports
```

# Decisions

## 1. Scope

I built everything the brief requires: the data model with migrations and a relative-date seed,
the priority queue, the state machine, the five endpoints, the Kitchen Display page, and the
required Jest tests. I also did all three extras: `POST /orders` with validation and tests, a
Vitest component test (empty state, and Cancel only on received orders), and a Playwright happy path.

I kept the code deliberately simple. There is no DI container, no class hierarchy and no
generic repository. The module takes its repository as a function argument, and that is the only
seam the tests need.

On top of the brief, I added a second compose file, `docker-compose-app.yml`. It runs the API and
web app in `node:22` containers, so the app runs with only Docker installed. `docker-compose.yml`
is exactly the Postgres-only file from section 9.3, and the four-command host flow still works.
Playwright runs on the host and reuses the apps if they are already running in Docker.

What I cut: there is no UI form for creating orders (the brief says API only), and there are no
API integration tests against a real Postgres. I checked the HTTP layer and the SQL by running the
app and calling it with curl, and the Playwright test covers the full path once.

## 2. Layers

- **Endpoint** (`ordersEndpoint.js`) reads `req`, calls the module and writes JSON. It contains no `if` about business rules.
- **Module** (`modules/`) holds every rule. `priority.js` has the scoring and the tie-break as pure
  functions. `orderStatus.js` has the transition table. `orderModule.js` holds the use cases
  (queue, status change, create) and turns a broken rule into an `AppError` with a stable code.
- **Repository** (`orderRepository.js`) holds all Sequelize code. It returns plain objects, so
  the modules never see a Sequelize instance, and tests swap in an in-memory fake with the same functions.
- **Schema** holds the models, the migration and the seed. The migration also adds CHECK
  constraints, so the database rejects an invalid status, type or quantity even if a bug gets past the app.
- **UI** renders what the API returns, in the order it returns it.

The rule I refused to put in the UI: **which actions are valid for an order.** The obvious
approach is a `status → button` map in React, but that is a second copy of the state machine.
When the product team changes a transition, someone would update the server and forget the UI.
Instead the API returns `allowed_actions` for each order, computed from the same `TRANSITIONS`
table the server enforces. The UI only knows button labels. The score works the same way: the UI
has no scoring code at all, it only displays `score`.

## 3. Priority

`GET /orders/queue` loads the orders in the requested statuses together with their items and the
items' prep times. The module then calls `rankOrders(orders, now)` with `now = new Date()`, taken
once per request in the endpoint. `rankOrders` adds a `score` to each order with
`calculateScore(order, now)` and sorts with `compareOrders`: score descending, then `promised_at`
(earlier first, nulls last), then `placed_at`, then `id`. Nothing is stored, so the score is
always current. Tests pass a frozen `now` (`2026-06-15T12:00:00Z`) and never touch the clock.

All the weights live in one `PRIORITY_RULES` object at the top of `priority.js`, so changing the
ranking usually means editing one value.

Edge cases that were easy to get wrong:

- **Whole minutes.** Wait time uses floored whole minutes, so 9m50s counts as 9 minutes and
  scores 0 points, not 5. Rounding the minutes, or flooring only once at the end of the formula,
  gives the wrong answer. There is a test for exactly this case.
- **The gap between "within 30" and "31–60".** A promise 30m30s away fits neither bucket if you
  read the brief literally. I compare exact (unfloored) minutes: up to 30 gives 25 points, up to
  60 gives 15, so 30m30s gives 15.
- **Overdue promises.** A `promised_at` in the past counts as "within 30 minutes" and gives 25
  points. A late order should not lose priority for being late.

## 4. Transitions

The state machine is the `TRANSITIONS` table in `api/src/modules/orderStatus.js`. The server
enforces it in `orderModule.changeStatus`, which every transition endpoint goes through:

1. Load the order. If it does not exist, return `ORDER_NOT_FOUND` (404).
2. Call `assertTransition(current, target)`. An illegal change returns `INVALID_TRANSITION` (409).
3. Write with a **conditional update** (`UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND status = <the status we checked>`).
   If no row changed, another request moved the order between our read and our write, so we
   return `INVALID_TRANSITION` instead of overwriting it.

Starting an order that is already `preparing` returns
`409 {"error":{"code":"INVALID_TRANSITION","message":"Cannot change order status from \"preparing\" to \"preparing\""}}`
and nothing in the database changes. The UI shows that message in a red alert above the table
and reloads the queue, because the screen was evidently stale.

## 5. AI

I used Claude Code for this exercise. The full conversation is in `ai-logs/`.

**Kept:** "make the status update conditional: `WHERE id = ? AND status = <expected from>`. If
0 rows update, return INVALID_TRANSITION." My first idea was read → check → update. That has a
gap: two expeditors clicking Start at the same moment would both pass the check. The
conditional update closes the gap with one extra `where` field and no locks or transactions.
`transitions.test.js` covers it by simulating a lost race.

**Rejected:** for my requirement that the only command should be `docker compose up`, the AI
proposed a `docker-compose.override.yml`, which Docker merges automatically. That would make
`docker compose up -d` (step 1 of the brief) quietly start the API and web app too. That breaks
section 9.3, and the reviewer's `npm run dev` would then fail on ports already in use. I chose an
explicit `docker-compose-app.yml` instead: the brief's flow stays exactly as written, and the
Docker-only flow is one extra, visible `-f` flag.

**Also rewritten:** the AI first suggested skipping Playwright because running browsers inside
Docker is heavy. I kept the test and moved it to the host instead. `reuseExistingServer` lets it
work against either the Docker-hosted apps or apps it starts itself.

## 6. Next

1. **Status history with timestamps and the person who made each change.** Add an
   `order_status_events` table written in the same transaction as the status change. A real
   kitchen needs to answer "why was this order late?" and "who cancelled it?". It also unlocks
   ranking by time spent in `preparing`, a likely next product request.
2. **Push updates to every screen.** Several screens (expeditor, line cooks, pass) must agree
   within seconds. Today each screen polls every 30 seconds, and a stale screen only finds out
   when a click returns 409. I would push changes to the screens (Server-Sent Events) and keep
   the conditional update as the safety net.

# Kitchen Display Queue

An internal tool for a restaurant kitchen: the expeditor sees every active order ranked by a
priority score and moves each order through its preparation stages.

- **API**: Node.js 22, Express 5, Sequelize 6 (migrations), PostgreSQL 16, Jest — `api/`
- **Web**: Vite, React 19, TypeScript, MUI 7, Vitest, Playwright — `web/`

| Service    | Port |
| ---------- | ---- |
| API        | 4000 |
| Web        | 5173 |
| PostgreSQL | 5433 (host) → 5432 (container) |

## Getting started

Prerequisites: **Docker**. Node 22 is only needed for option B and for the Playwright e2e test.

### Option A — Docker only (no Node on the host)

```bash
docker compose up -d                              # 1. Postgres (docker-compose.yml)
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml up       # 2. API + web in Node 22 containers
```

The API container runs `npm install`, the migrations and the seed every time it starts, so each
start gives fresh demo data with dates relative to now. Open http://localhost:5173.

Run the unit tests inside the containers (while they are running):

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml exec api npm test
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml exec web npm test
```

### Option B — Node 22 on the host

```bash
docker compose up -d     # 1. start Postgres
npm install              # 2. installs the root, api/ and web/ dependencies
npm run db:setup         # 3. runs migrations + seed
npm run dev              # 4. starts the API and the web app
```

Do not run both options at the same time: they use the same ports.

## Tests

```bash
npm test                 # Jest (api) + Vitest (web); no database needed
```

- `api/tests/priority.test.js`: the scoring formula, both caps, every promised-time bucket, and the tie-break. All use a frozen `now`.
- `api/tests/transitions.test.js`: every legal and illegal status change, and the queue contents. Uses an in-memory repository.
- `api/tests/createOrder.test.js`: `POST /orders` validation.
- `web/src/components/QueueTable.test.tsx`: the empty state, and that Cancel appears only for received orders.

### End-to-end (Playwright, runs on the host)

```bash
docker compose up -d                          # Postgres must be running
npm install                                   # once
npx --prefix web playwright install chromium  # once
npm run test:e2e
```

If the apps are already running (from option A or B), Playwright reuses them. Otherwise it
re-seeds the database and starts them itself. If no `received` orders are left, run
`npm run db:setup` (or restart the API container) to reset the demo data.

## API

| Method | Path                  | Behavior |
| ------ | --------------------- | -------- |
| GET    | `/orders/queue`       | Active queue (`received` + `preparing`) sorted by score. `?status=received` or `?status=preparing` to filter. Each order includes `score`, `minutes_waiting` and `allowed_actions`. |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/start`   | `received` → `preparing` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/ready`   | `preparing` → `ready` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/pickup`  | `ready` → `picked_up` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/cancel`  | `received` → `cancelled` |
| POST   | `/orders`             | Create an order: `{ customer_name, type, is_vip?, promised_at?, items: [{ menu_item_id, quantity }] }` |

### Error codes

Every error response has the shape `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`.

| Code                    | HTTP | When |
| ----------------------- | ---- | ---- |
| `INVALID_TRANSITION`    | 409  | The status change is not allowed from the current status. This includes repeating a step, skipping a step, changing a terminal order, or losing a race with another request. |
| `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`       | 404  | No order with that id (or the id is not a positive integer). |
| `INVALID_STATUS_FILTER` | 400  | `status` query parameter is not `received` or `preparing`. |
| `VALIDATION_ERROR`      | 400  | `POST /orders` body is invalid, or a `menu_item_id` does not exist. |
| `INVALID_JSON`          | 400  | Request body is not valid JSON. |
| `ROUTE_NOT_FOUND`       | 404  | Unknown path. |
| `INTERNAL_ERROR`        | 500  | Unexpected server error (details are logged, not returned). |

## Project layout

```
api/src/
  endpoints/ordersEndpoint.js      HTTP only
  modules/priority.js              pure scoring + ranking (rules at the top of the file)
  modules/orderStatus.js           state machine (transition table)
  modules/orderValidation.js       POST /orders shape validation
  modules/orderModule.js           use cases: queue, status change, create
  repositories/orderRepository.js  Sequelize queries
  schema/                          models, migration, seed, DB config
web/src/
  components/KitchenDisplay.tsx    page: filter, data loading, error message
  components/QueueTable.tsx        the table
  api.ts                           fetch wrapper
web/e2e/                           Playwright test
ai-logs/                           AI conversation exports
```

# Decisions

## 1. Scope

I built everything the brief requires: the data model with migrations and a relative-date seed,
the priority queue, the state machine, the five endpoints, the Kitchen Display page, and the
required Jest tests. I also did all three extras: `POST /orders` with validation and tests, a
Vitest component test (empty state, and Cancel only on received orders), and a Playwright happy path.

I kept the code deliberately simple. There is no DI container, no class hierarchy and no
generic repository. The module takes its repository as a function argument, and that is the only
seam the tests need.

On top of the brief, I added a second compose file, `docker-compose-app.yml`. It runs the API and
web app in `node:22` containers, so the app runs with only Docker installed. `docker-compose.yml`
is exactly the Postgres-only file from section 9.3, and the four-command host flow still works.
Playwright runs on the host and reuses the apps if they are already running in Docker.

What I cut: there is no UI form for creating orders (the brief says API only), and there are no
API integration tests against a real Postgres. I checked the HTTP layer and the SQL by running the
app and calling it with curl, and the Playwright test covers the full path once.

## 2. Layers

- **Endpoint** (`ordersEndpoint.js`) reads `req`, calls the module and writes JSON. It contains no `if` about business rules.
- **Module** (`modules/`) holds every rule. `priority.js` has the scoring and the tie-break as pure
  functions. `orderStatus.js` has the transition table. `orderModule.js` holds the use cases
  (queue, status change, create) and turns a broken rule into an `AppError` with a stable code.
- **Repository** (`orderRepository.js`) holds all Sequelize code. It returns plain objects, so
  the modules never see a Sequelize instance, and tests swap in an in-memory fake with the same functions.
- **Schema** holds the models, the migration and the seed. The migration also adds CHECK
  constraints, so the database rejects an invalid status, type or quantity even if a bug gets past the app.
- **UI** renders what the API returns, in the order it returns it.

The rule I refused to put in the UI: **which actions are valid for an order.** The obvious
approach is a `status → button` map in React, but that is a second copy of the state machine.
When the product team changes a transition, someone would update the server and forget the UI.
Instead the API returns `allowed_actions` for each order, computed from the same `TRANSITIONS`
table the server enforces. The UI only knows button labels. The score works the same way: the UI
has no scoring code at all, it only displays `score`.

## 3. Priority

`GET /orders/queue` loads the orders in the requested statuses together with their items and the
items' prep times. The module then calls `rankOrders(orders, now)` with `now = new Date()`, taken
once per request in the endpoint. `rankOrders` adds a `score` to each order with
`calculateScore(order, now)` and sorts with `compareOrders`: score descending, then `promised_at`
(earlier first, nulls last), then `placed_at`, then `id`. Nothing is stored, so the score is
always current. Tests pass a frozen `now` (`2026-06-15T12:00:00Z`) and never touch the clock.

All the weights live in one `PRIORITY_RULES` object at the top of `priority.js`, so changing the
ranking usually means editing one value.

Edge cases that were easy to get wrong:

- **Whole minutes.** Wait time uses floored whole minutes, so 9m50s counts as 9 minutes and
  scores 0 points, not 5. Rounding the minutes, or flooring only once at the end of the formula,
  gives the wrong answer. There is a test for exactly this case.
- **The gap between "within 30" and "31–60".** A promise 30m30s away fits neither bucket if you
  read the brief literally. I compare exact (unfloored) minutes: up to 30 gives 25 points, up to
  60 gives 15, so 30m30s gives 15.
- **Overdue promises.** A `promised_at` in the past counts as "within 30 minutes" and gives 25
  points. A late order should not lose priority for being late.

## 4. Transitions

The state machine is the `TRANSITIONS` table in `api/src/modules/orderStatus.js`. The server
enforces it in `orderModule.changeStatus`, which every transition endpoint goes through:

1. Load the order. If it does not exist, return `ORDER_NOT_FOUND` (404).
2. Call `assertTransition(current, target)`. An illegal change returns `INVALID_TRANSITION` (409).
3. Write with a **conditional update** (`UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND status = <the status we checked>`).
   If no row changed, another request moved the order between our read and our write, so we
   return `INVALID_TRANSITION` instead of overwriting it.

Starting an order that is already `preparing` returns
`409 {"error":{"code":"INVALID_TRANSITION","message":"Cannot change order status from \"preparing\" to \"preparing\""}}`
and nothing in the database changes. The UI shows that message in a red alert above the table
and reloads the queue, because the screen was evidently stale.

## 5. AI

I used Claude Code for this exercise. The full conversation is in `ai-logs/`.

**Kept:** "make the status update conditional: `WHERE id = ? AND status = <expected from>`. If
0 rows update, return INVALID_TRANSITION." My first idea was read → check → update. That has a

conditional update closes the gap with one extra `where` field and no locks or transactions.

**Also rewritten:** the AI first suggested skipping Playwright because running browsers inside
Docker is heavy. I kept the test and moved it to the host instead. `reuseExistingServer` lets it
work against either the Docker-hosted apps or apps it starts itself.

   `order_status_events` table written in the same transaction as the status change. A real
   kitchen needs to answer "why was this order late?" and "who cancelled it?". It also unlocks
   ranking by time spent in `preparing`, a likely next product request.

The project is built, all tests pass, and the app is running from Docker now at **http://localhost:5173**.

**What I checked:**
- **API tests:** 89 Jest tests pass. They cover the scoring, both caps, every promised-time bucket, the tie-break, all transitions, and `POST /orders` validation.
- **Web tests:** 3 Vitest tests pass, and the TypeScript type check is clean.
- **Playwright:** passes on your machine in both setups: against the apps running in Docker, and with Playwright starting the apps itself.
- **Real API:** I called it with curl. The seeded scores match the comments in the seed file (75/70/60/60/50/50/15), both ties break correctly, and every error code comes back as documented.

**How to run it:**
- `docker compose up -d` starts Postgres only; that file matches section 9.3 exactly.
- `docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml up` starts the API and web app in Node 22 containers. The API runs migrations and re-seeds on every start.
- The four-command flow from the brief (`npm install`, `db:setup`, `dev`) still works for reviewers who use Node on their machine.
- Playwright runs on your machine with `npm run test:e2e`.

**Where the rules live (the interview's live-change area):**
- **Ranking:** all the weights are in the `PRIORITY_RULES` object in `api/src/modules/priority.js`; the tie-break is in `compareOrders` in the same file.
- **Status rules:** the `TRANSITIONS` table in `api/src/modules/orderStatus.js`. The UI gets each order's valid actions from the API, so a status change needs no UI edit.

content.text:
Here's the plan, kept simple:

- **API:** add `GET /menu-items`, because the form needs the menu items to choose from. It follows the same layers: endpoint → module → repository.
- **Web:**
  - a floating **+** button (MUI Fab) that opens a "New order" dialog
  - the dialog takes customer name, type, VIP, "promised in N minutes" and item rows
  - the server stays the only validator, and its errors appear inside the dialog
- **Auto refresh:** poll every 5 seconds instead of 30, quietly with no loading bar flicker, and skip polls while the tab is hidden. A newer response can't be overwritten by an older one that arrives late. The page shows an "updated hh:mm:ss" time.
- **Tests:** Vitest for the dialog (correct payload, API error shown) and for the display (a background refresh shows a new order, a transition error is visible), plus a Playwright test that creates an order through the dialog.

I'll use an inline SVG for the + icon instead of adding `@mui/icons-material`, which is large and Docker's disk is tight.

# Kitchen Display Queue

An internal tool for a restaurant kitchen: the expeditor sees every active order ranked by a
priority score and moves each order through its preparation stages.

- **API**: Node.js 22, Express 5, Sequelize 6 (migrations), PostgreSQL 16, Jest — `api/`
- **Web**: Vite, React 19, TypeScript, MUI 7, Vitest, Playwright — `web/`

| Service    | Port |
| ---------- | ---- |
| API        | 4000 |
| Web        | 5173 |
| PostgreSQL | 5433 (host) → 5432 (container) |

## Getting started

Prerequisites: **Docker**. Node 22 is only needed for option B and for the Playwright e2e test.

### Option A — Docker only (no Node on the host)

```bash
docker compose up -d                              # 1. Postgres (docker-compose.yml)
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml up       # 2. API + web in Node 22 containers
```

The API container runs `npm install`, the migrations and the seed every time it starts, so each
start gives fresh demo data with dates relative to now. Open http://localhost:5173.

Run the unit tests inside the containers (while they are running):

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml exec api npm test
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml exec web npm test
```

### Option B — Node 22 on the host

```bash
docker compose up -d     # 1. start Postgres
npm install              # 2. installs the root, api/ and web/ dependencies
npm run db:setup         # 3. runs migrations + seed
npm run dev              # 4. starts the API and the web app
```

Do not run both options at the same time: they use the same ports.

## Tests

```bash
npm test                 # Jest (api) + Vitest (web); no database needed
```

- `api/tests/priority.test.js`: the scoring formula, both caps, every promised-time bucket, and the tie-break. All use a frozen `now`.
- `api/tests/transitions.test.js`: every legal and illegal status change, and the queue contents. Uses an in-memory repository.
- `api/tests/createOrder.test.js`: `POST /orders` validation.
- `web/src/components/QueueTable.test.tsx`: the empty state, and that Cancel appears only for received orders.

### End-to-end (Playwright, runs on the host)

```bash
docker compose up -d                          # Postgres must be running
npm install                                   # once
npx --prefix web playwright install chromium  # once
npm run test:e2e
```

If the apps are already running (from option A or B), Playwright reuses them. Otherwise it
re-seeds the database and starts them itself. If no `received` orders are left, run
`npm run db:setup` (or restart the API container) to reset the demo data.

## API

| Method | Path                  | Behavior |
| ------ | --------------------- | -------- |
| GET    | `/orders/queue`       | Active queue (`received` + `preparing`) sorted by score. `?status=received` or `?status=preparing` to filter. Each order includes `score`, `minutes_waiting` and `allowed_actions`. |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/start`   | `received` → `preparing` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/ready`   | `preparing` → `ready` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/pickup`  | `ready` → `picked_up` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/cancel`  | `received` → `cancelled` |
| POST   | `/orders`             | Create an order: `{ customer_name, type, is_vip?, promised_at?, items: [{ menu_item_id, quantity }] }` |

### Error codes

Every error response has the shape `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`.

| Code                    | HTTP | When |
| ----------------------- | ---- | ---- |
| `INVALID_TRANSITION`    | 409  | The status change is not allowed from the current status. This includes repeating a step, skipping a step, changing a terminal order, or losing a race with another request. |
| `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`       | 404  | No order with that id (or the id is not a positive integer). |
| `INVALID_STATUS_FILTER` | 400  | `status` query parameter is not `received` or `preparing`. |
| `VALIDATION_ERROR`      | 400  | `POST /orders` body is invalid, or a `menu_item_id` does not exist. |
| `INVALID_JSON`          | 400  | Request body is not valid JSON. |
| `ROUTE_NOT_FOUND`       | 404  | Unknown path. |
| `INTERNAL_ERROR`        | 500  | Unexpected server error (details are logged, not returned). |

## Project layout

```
api/src/
  endpoints/ordersEndpoint.js      HTTP only
  modules/priority.js              pure scoring + ranking (rules at the top of the file)
  modules/orderStatus.js           state machine (transition table)
  modules/orderValidation.js       POST /orders shape validation
  modules/orderModule.js           use cases: queue, status change, create
  repositories/orderRepository.js  Sequelize queries
  schema/                          models, migration, seed, DB config
web/src/
  components/KitchenDisplay.tsx    page: filter, data loading, error message
  components/QueueTable.tsx        the table
  api.ts                           fetch wrapper
web/e2e/                           Playwright test
ai-logs/                           AI conversation exports
```

# Decisions

## 1. Scope

I built everything the brief requires: the data model with migrations and a relative-date seed,
the priority queue, the state machine, the five endpoints, the Kitchen Display page, and the
required Jest tests. I also did all three extras: `POST /orders` with validation and tests, a
Vitest component test (empty state, and Cancel only on received orders), and a Playwright happy path.

I kept the code deliberately simple. There is no DI container, no class hierarchy and no
generic repository. The module takes its repository as a function argument, and that is the only
seam the tests need.

On top of the brief, I added a second compose file, `docker-compose-app.yml`. It runs the API and
web app in `node:22` containers, so the app runs with only Docker installed. `docker-compose.yml`
is exactly the Postgres-only file from section 9.3, and the four-command host flow still works.
Playwright runs on the host and reuses the apps if they are already running in Docker.

What I cut: there is no UI form for creating orders (the brief says API only), and there are no
API integration tests against a real Postgres. I checked the HTTP layer and the SQL by running the
app and calling it with curl, and the Playwright test covers the full path once.

## 2. Layers

- **Endpoint** (`ordersEndpoint.js`) reads `req`, calls the module and writes JSON. It contains no `if` about business rules.
- **Module** (`modules/`) holds every rule. `priority.js` has the scoring and the tie-break as pure
  functions. `orderStatus.js` has the transition table. `orderModule.js` holds the use cases
  (queue, status change, create) and turns a broken rule into an `AppError` with a stable code.
- **Repository** (`orderRepository.js`) holds all Sequelize code. It returns plain objects, so
  the modules never see a Sequelize instance, and tests swap in an in-memory fake with the same functions.
- **Schema** holds the models, the migration and the seed. The migration also adds CHECK
  constraints, so the database rejects an invalid status, type or quantity even if a bug gets past the app.
- **UI** renders what the API returns, in the order it returns it.

The rule I refused to put in the UI: **which actions are valid for an order.** The obvious
approach is a `status → button` map in React, but that is a second copy of the state machine.
When the product team changes a transition, someone would update the server and forget the UI.
Instead the API returns `allowed_actions` for each order, computed from the same `TRANSITIONS`
table the server enforces. The UI only knows button labels. The score works the same way: the UI
has no scoring code at all, it only displays `score`.

## 3. Priority

`GET /orders/queue` loads the orders in the requested statuses together with their items and the
items' prep times. The module then calls `rankOrders(orders, now)` with `now = new Date()`, taken
once per request in the endpoint. `rankOrders` adds a `score` to each order with
`calculateScore(order, now)` and sorts with `compareOrders`: score descending, then `promised_at`
(earlier first, nulls last), then `placed_at`, then `id`. Nothing is stored, so the score is
always current. Tests pass a frozen `now` (`2026-06-15T12:00:00Z`) and never touch the clock.

All the weights live in one `PRIORITY_RULES` object at the top of `priority.js`, so changing the
ranking usually means editing one value.

Edge cases that were easy to get wrong:

- **Whole minutes.** Wait time uses floored whole minutes, so 9m50s counts as 9 minutes and
  scores 0 points, not 5. Rounding the minutes, or flooring only once at the end of the formula,
  gives the wrong answer. There is a test for exactly this case.
- **The gap between "within 30" and "31–60".** A promise 30m30s away fits neither bucket if you
  read the brief literally. I compare exact (unfloored) minutes: up to 30 gives 25 points, up to
  60 gives 15, so 30m30s gives 15.
- **Overdue promises.** A `promised_at` in the past counts as "within 30 minutes" and gives 25
  points. A late order should not lose priority for being late.

## 4. Transitions

The state machine is the `TRANSITIONS` table in `api/src/modules/orderStatus.js`. The server
enforces it in `orderModule.changeStatus`, which every transition endpoint goes through:

1. Load the order. If it does not exist, return `ORDER_NOT_FOUND` (404).
2. Call `assertTransition(current, target)`. An illegal change returns `INVALID_TRANSITION` (409).
3. Write with a **conditional update** (`UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND status = <the status we checked>`).
   If no row changed, another request moved the order between our read and our write, so we
   return `INVALID_TRANSITION` instead of overwriting it.

Starting an order that is already `preparing` returns
`409 {"error":{"code":"INVALID_TRANSITION","message":"Cannot change order status from \"preparing\" to \"preparing\""}}`
and nothing in the database changes. The UI shows that message in a red alert above the table
and reloads the queue, because the screen was evidently stale.

## 5. AI

I used Claude Code for this exercise. The full conversation is in `ai-logs/`.

**Kept:** "make the status update conditional: `WHERE id = ? AND status = <expected from>`. If
0 rows update, return INVALID_TRANSITION." A plain read → check → update has a gap: two
expeditors clicking Start at the same moment would both pass the check. The
conditional update closes the gap with one extra `where` field and no locks or transactions.
`transitions.test.js` covers it by simulating a lost race.

**Rejected:** for my requirement that the only command should be `docker compose up`, the AI
proposed a `docker-compose.override.yml`, which Docker merges automatically. That would make
`docker compose up -d` (step 1 of the brief) quietly start the API and web app too. That breaks
section 9.3, and the reviewer's `npm run dev` would then fail on ports already in use. I chose an
explicit `docker-compose-app.yml` instead: the brief's flow stays exactly as written, and the
Docker-only flow is one extra, visible `-f` flag.

**Also rewritten:** the AI first suggested skipping Playwright because running browsers inside
Docker is heavy. I kept the test and moved it to the host instead. `reuseExistingServer` lets it
work against either the Docker-hosted apps or apps it starts itself.

## 6. Next

1. **Status history with timestamps and the person who made each change.** Add an
   `order_status_events` table written in the same transaction as the status change. A real
   kitchen needs to answer "why was this order late?" and "who cancelled it?". It also unlocks
   ranking by time spent in `preparing`, a likely next product request.
2. **Push updates to every screen.** Several screens (expeditor, line cooks, pass) must agree

# Decisions

## 1. Scope

I built everything the brief requires: the data model with migrations and a relative-date seed,
the priority queue, the state machine, the five endpoints, the Kitchen Display page, and the
required Jest tests. I also did all three extras: `POST /orders` with validation and tests, a
Vitest component test (empty state, and Cancel only on received orders), and a Playwright happy path.

Beyond the extras, I added two things that are not in the brief:

- **A "New order" UI.** The brief says no UI form is needed for `POST /orders`, but without one
  the feature can only be used with curl, which felt incomplete. A floating + button opens a
  dialog. It needed one small read-only endpoint, `GET /menu-items`, to fill the item picker.
- **Background auto-refresh every 5 seconds.** New orders created elsewhere appear without a page
  reload, and scores stay current as wait times grow.

I kept the code deliberately simple. There is no DI container, no class hierarchy and no
generic repository. The module takes its repository as a function argument, and that is the only
seam the tests need.

On top of the brief, I added a second compose file, `docker-compose-app.yml`. It runs the API and
web app in `node:22` containers, so the app runs with only Docker installed. `docker-compose.yml`
is exactly the Postgres-only file from section 9.3, and the four-command host flow still works.
Playwright runs on the host and reuses the apps if they are already running in Docker.

What I cut: there is no UI form for creating orders (the brief says API only), and there are no
API integration tests against a real Postgres. I checked the HTTP layer and the SQL by running the
app and calling it with curl, and the Playwright test covers the full path once.

## 2. Layers

- **Endpoint** (`ordersEndpoint.js`) reads `req`, calls the module and writes JSON. It contains no `if` about business rules.
- **Module** (`modules/`) holds every rule. `priority.js` has the scoring and the tie-break as pure
  functions. `orderStatus.js` has the transition table. `orderModule.js` holds the use cases
  (queue, status change, create) and turns a broken rule into an `AppError` with a stable code.
- **Repository** (`orderRepository.js`) holds all Sequelize code. It returns plain objects, so
  the modules never see a Sequelize instance, and tests swap in an in-memory fake with the same functions.
- **Schema** holds the models, the migration and the seed. The migration also adds CHECK
  constraints, so the database rejects an invalid status, type or quantity even if a bug gets past the app.
- **UI** renders what the API returns, in the order it returns it.

The rule I refused to put in the UI: **which actions are valid for an order.** The obvious
approach is a `status → button` map in React, but that is a second copy of the state machine.
When the product team changes a transition, someone would update the server and forget the UI.
Instead the API returns `allowed_actions` for each order, computed from the same `TRANSITIONS`
table the server enforces. The UI only knows button labels. The score works the same way: the UI
has no scoring code at all, it only displays `score`.

## 3. Priority

`GET /orders/queue` loads the orders in the requested statuses together with their items and the
items' prep times. The module then calls `rankOrders(orders, now)` with `now = new Date()`, taken
once per request in the endpoint. `rankOrders` adds a `score` to each order with
`calculateScore(order, now)` and sorts with `compareOrders`: score descending, then `promised_at`
(earlier first, nulls last), then `placed_at`, then `id`. Nothing is stored, so the score is
always current. Tests pass a frozen `now` (`2026-06-15T12:00:00Z`) and never touch the clock.

All the weights live in one `PRIORITY_RULES` object at the top of `priority.js`, so changing the
ranking usually means editing one value.

Edge cases that were easy to get wrong:

- **Whole minutes.** Wait time uses floored whole minutes, so 9m50s counts as 9 minutes and
  scores 0 points, not 5. Rounding the minutes, or flooring only once at the end of the formula,
  gives the wrong answer. There is a test for exactly this case.
- **The gap between "within 30" and "31–60".** A promise 30m30s away fits neither bucket if you
  read the brief literally. I compare exact (unfloored) minutes: up to 30 gives 25 points, up to
  60 gives 15, so 30m30s gives 15.
- **Overdue promises.** A `promised_at` in the past counts as "within 30 minutes" and gives 25
  points. A late order should not lose priority for being late.

## 4. Transitions

The state machine is the `TRANSITIONS` table in `api/src/modules/orderStatus.js`. The server
enforces it in `orderModule.changeStatus`, which every transition endpoint goes through:

1. Load the order. If it does not exist, return `ORDER_NOT_FOUND` (404).
2. Call `assertTransition(current, target)`. An illegal change returns `INVALID_TRANSITION` (409).
3. Write with a **conditional update** (`UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND status = <the status we checked>`).
   If no row changed, another request moved the order between our read and our write, so we
   return `INVALID_TRANSITION` instead of overwriting it.

Starting an order that is already `preparing` returns
`409 {"error":{"code":"INVALID_TRANSITION","message":"Cannot change order status from \"preparing\" to \"preparing\""}}`
and nothing in the database changes. The UI shows that message in a red alert above the table
and reloads the queue, because the screen was evidently stale.

## 5. AI

I used Claude Code for this exercise. The full conversation is in `ai-logs/`.

**Kept:** "make the status update conditional: `WHERE id = ? AND status = <expected from>`. If
0 rows update, return INVALID_TRANSITION." A plain read → check → update has a gap: two
expeditors clicking Start at the same moment would both pass the check. The
conditional update closes the gap with one extra `where` field and no locks or transactions.
`transitions.test.js` covers it by simulating a lost race.

**Rejected:** for my requirement that the only command should be `docker compose up`, the AI
proposed a `docker-compose.override.yml`, which Docker merges automatically. That would make
`docker compose up -d` (step 1 of the brief) quietly start the API and web app too. That breaks
section 9.3, and the reviewer's `npm run dev` would then fail on ports already in use. I chose an
explicit `docker-compose-app.yml` instead: the brief's flow stays exactly as written, and the
Docker-only flow is one extra, visible `-f` flag.

**Also rewritten:** the AI first suggested skipping Playwright because running browsers inside
Docker is heavy. I kept the test and moved it to the host instead. `reuseExistingServer` lets it
work against either the Docker-hosted apps or apps it starts itself.

## 6. Next

1. **Status history with timestamps and the person who made each change.** Add an
   `order_status_events` table written in the same transaction as the status change. A real
   kitchen needs to answer "why was this order late?" and "who cancelled it?". It also unlocks
   ranking by time spent in `preparing`, a likely next product request.
2. **Push updates to every screen.** Several screens (expeditor, line cooks, pass) must agree
   within seconds. Today each screen polls every 30 seconds, and a stale screen only finds out
   when a click returns 409. I would push changes to the screens (Server-Sent Events) and keep
   the conditional update as the safety net.

The New order UI and the background auto-refresh are in, and all tests pass:

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| Jest (API) | 90 passed |
| Vitest (web) | 9 passed (was 3) |
| Playwright | 2 passed |
| TypeScript check | clean |

I also checked both features in the running Docker app with screenshots.

**New order (floating + button):**
- The + button opens a dialog with customer name, type, "promised in N minutes", VIP, and item rows you can add and remove.
- The form doesn't validate anything itself. The server's `VALIDATION_ERROR` messages appear inside the dialog, so validation rules exist only on the server.
- After an order is created, the dialog closes, a short confirmation message appears, and the queue reloads.
- The item picker needed a new endpoint, `GET /menu-items`. It follows the same layers as the rest: endpoint → `menuModule` → `menuItemRepository`.

**Auto-refresh:**
- The queue reloads every 5 seconds (it was 30) without flashing the progress bar.
- It pauses while the browser tab is hidden.
- The header shows "updated hh:mm:ss".
- Only the newest request can update the table. Without that, a slow response for the old filter could overwrite the results after you switch filters.

**New tests:**
- **Dialog:** sends the correct payload, shows an API error, adds and removes item rows.
- **Display:** a background refresh shows an order that arrived later, a rejected transition shows the red alert, and the + button opens the dialog.
- **Playwright:** creates an order through the + button and checks it appears in the queue.
- **API:** a small test for the menu module.

**Fixed while checking screenshots:**
- The "Menu item" label was drawn on top of "Choose…"; I pinned the labels above both dropdowns.
- I added bottom padding so the + button can't cover the last row's buttons.

**Docs:**
- `README.md` now covers the new endpoint, a UI section and the new tests.
- `DECISIONS.md` lists both additions under Scope, explains in Layers why the form doesn't validate, and its "Next" section now refers to 5-second polling.

# Sample requests for the Kitchen Display Queue API.
# Use with the VS Code "REST Client" extension (humao.rest-client): click "Send Request" above each one.
#
# Tip: run "Create an order" first. The transition requests below use its id
# ({{createOrder.response.body.order.id}}), so you can walk one order through its whole life.

@baseUrl = http://localhost:4000

###############################################################################
# Queue
###############################################################################

### Active queue (received + preparing), sorted by score
GET {{baseUrl}}/orders/queue

### Only received orders
GET {{baseUrl}}/orders/queue?status=received

### Only preparing orders
GET {{baseUrl}}/orders/queue?status=preparing

### Invalid filter -> 400 INVALID_STATUS_FILTER
GET {{baseUrl}}/orders/queue?status=ready

###############################################################################
# Menu
###############################################################################

### Menu items (ids to use in POST /orders)
GET {{baseUrl}}/menu-items

###############################################################################
# Create orders
###############################################################################

### Create an order (VIP delivery promised in the future)
# @name createOrder
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "customer_name": "REST Client",
  "type": "delivery",
  "is_vip": true,
  "promised_at": "{{$datetime iso8601 20 m}}",
  "items": [
    { "menu_item_id": 1, "quantity": 2 },
    { "menu_item_id": 4, "quantity": 1 }
  ]
}

### Create a minimal order (dine-in, no promise, not VIP)
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "customer_name": "Walk-in",
  "type": "dine_in",
  "items": [{ "menu_item_id": 2, "quantity": 1 }]
}

### Validation error: empty items -> 400 VALIDATION_ERROR
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "customer_name": "Nobody",
  "type": "takeout",
  "items": []
}

### Validation error: several problems at once -> 400 VALIDATION_ERROR
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "customer_name": "",
  "type": "drive_thru",
  "promised_at": "tomorrow",
  "items": [{ "menu_item_id": 1, "quantity": 0 }]
}

### Validation error: menu item does not exist -> 400 VALIDATION_ERROR
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "customer_name": "Ghost",
  "type": "takeout",
  "items": [{ "menu_item_id": 999, "quantity": 1 }]
}

### Malformed JSON -> 400 INVALID_JSON
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders
Content-Type: application/json

{ "customer_name": "oops",

###############################################################################
# Status transitions (uses the order created by "createOrder" above)
###############################################################################

@orderId = {{createOrder.response.body.order.id}}

### received -> preparing
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders/{{orderId}}/start

### Start again -> 409 INVALID_TRANSITION (repeating a step is an error)
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders/{{orderId}}/start

### Cancel while preparing -> 409 INVALID_TRANSITION (only received orders can be cancelled)
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders/{{orderId}}/cancel

### preparing -> ready
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders/{{orderId}}/ready

### ready -> picked_up
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders/{{orderId}}/pickup

### Anything after picked_up -> 409 INVALID_TRANSITION (terminal status)
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders/{{orderId}}/start

###############################################################################
# Cancel flow (creates its own order)
###############################################################################

### Create an order to cancel
# @name orderToCancel
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "customer_name": "Changed my mind",
  "type": "takeout",
  "items": [{ "menu_item_id": 3, "quantity": 1 }]
}

### received -> cancelled
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders/{{orderToCancel.response.body.order.id}}/cancel

### Skip a step on a fresh order: received -> ready -> 409 INVALID_TRANSITION
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders/{{createOrder.response.body.order.id}}/ready

###############################################################################
# Not found
###############################################################################

### Unknown order -> 404 ORDER_NOT_FOUND
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders/999999/start

### Non-numeric id -> 404 ORDER_NOT_FOUND
POST {{baseUrl}}/orders/abc/start

### Unknown route -> 404 ROUTE_NOT_FOUND
GET {{baseUrl}}/nope

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# Kitchen Display Queue

An internal tool for a restaurant kitchen: the expeditor sees every active order ranked by a
priority score and moves each order through its preparation stages.

- **API**: Node.js 22, Express 5, Sequelize 6 (migrations), PostgreSQL 16, Jest — `api/`
- **Web**: Vite, React 19, TypeScript, MUI 7, Vitest, Playwright — `web/`

| Service    | Port |
| ---------- | ---- |
| API        | 4000 |
| Web        | 5173 |
| PostgreSQL | 5433 (host) → 5432 (container) |

## Getting started

Prerequisites: **Docker**. Node 22 is only needed for option B and for the Playwright e2e test.

### Option A — Docker only (no Node on the host)

```bash
docker compose up -d                              # 1. Postgres (docker-compose.yml)
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml up       # 2. API + web in Node 22 containers
```

The API container runs `npm install`, the migrations and the seed every time it starts, so each
start gives fresh demo data with dates relative to now. Open http://localhost:5173.

Run the unit tests inside the containers (while they are running):

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml exec api npm test
docker compose -f docker-compose-app.yml exec web npm test
```

### Option B — Node 22 on the host

```bash
docker compose up -d     # 1. start Postgres
npm install              # 2. installs the root, api/ and web/ dependencies
npm run db:setup         # 3. runs migrations + seed
npm run dev              # 4. starts the API and the web app
```

Do not run both options at the same time: they use the same ports.

## Tests

```bash
npm test                 # Jest (api) + Vitest (web); no database needed
```

- `api/tests/priority.test.js`: the scoring formula, both caps, every promised-time bucket, and the tie-break. All use a frozen `now`.
- `api/tests/transitions.test.js`: every legal and illegal status change, and the queue contents. Uses an in-memory repository.
- `api/tests/createOrder.test.js`: `POST /orders` validation.
- `api/tests/menu.test.js`: the menu listing.
- `web/src/components/QueueTable.test.tsx`: the empty state, Cancel only for received orders, and rows kept in API order.
- `web/src/components/KitchenDisplay.test.tsx`: a background refresh shows a new order, a rejected transition shows an error, and the + button opens the dialog.
- `web/src/components/NewOrderDialog.test.tsx`: the form sends the right payload, an API validation error is shown, and item rows can be added and removed.
- `web/e2e/`: start a seeded order, and create an order through the + button.

### End-to-end (Playwright, runs on the host)

```bash
docker compose up -d                          # Postgres must be running
npm install                                   # once
npx --prefix web playwright install chromium  # once
npm run test:e2e
```

If the apps are already running (from option A or B), Playwright reuses them. Otherwise it
re-seeds the database and starts them itself. If no `received` orders are left, run
`npm run db:setup` (or restart the API container) to reset the demo data.

## API

| Method | Path                  | Behavior |
| ------ | --------------------- | -------- |
| GET    | `/orders/queue`       | Active queue (`received` + `preparing`) sorted by score. `?status=received` or `?status=preparing` to filter. Each order includes `score`, `minutes_waiting` and `allowed_actions`. |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/start`   | `received` → `preparing` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/ready`   | `preparing` → `ready` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/pickup`  | `ready` → `picked_up` |
| POST   | `/orders/:id/cancel`  | `received` → `cancelled` |
| POST   | `/orders`             | Create an order: `{ customer_name, type, is_vip?, promised_at?, items: [{ menu_item_id, quantity }] }` |
| GET    | `/menu-items`         | The menu (feeds the "New order" form). |

## UI

- The queue table with a filter (Active / Received / Preparing). Each row shows the actions the API allows for it, and errors appear in a red alert.
- **Auto-refresh** every 5 seconds, in the background (no progress bar). It picks up orders created elsewhere and keeps the scores current, and it pauses while the browser tab is hidden.
- **New order**: the floating **+** button opens a dialog (customer, type, VIP, "promised in N minutes", item rows). The API validates the order and any error is shown inside the dialog.

### Error codes

Every error response has the shape `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`.

| Code                    | HTTP | When |
| ----------------------- | ---- | ---- |
| `INVALID_TRANSITION`    | 409  | The status change is not allowed from the current status. This includes repeating a step, skipping a step, changing a terminal order, or losing a race with another request. |
| `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`       | 404  | No order with that id (or the id is not a positive integer). |
| `INVALID_STATUS_FILTER` | 400  | `status` query parameter is not `received` or `preparing`. |
| `VALIDATION_ERROR`      | 400  | `POST /orders` body is invalid, or a `menu_item_id` does not exist. |
| `INVALID_JSON`          | 400  | Request body is not valid JSON. |
| `ROUTE_NOT_FOUND`       | 404  | Unknown path. |
| `INTERNAL_ERROR`        | 500  | Unexpected server error (details are logged, not returned). |

## Project layout

```
api/src/
  endpoints/ordersEndpoint.js      HTTP only
  modules/priority.js              pure scoring + ranking (rules at the top of the file)
  modules/orderStatus.js           state machine (transition table)
```

content.text:
Item 5 defines the sorting fully:

1. **Priority score**, highest first.
2. **Tie-break (5.2):** earlier `promised_at` first, with no promise last; then earlier `placed_at` first, which means the longest-waiting order first; then smaller `id`.

So Waiting and Promised already play a part in the order, as tie-breaks after the score. VIP counts only through its +20 score points, not as a separate sort key. Adding other sort keys would contradict item 5.

The code already implements exactly this (`compareOrders` in `api/src/modules/priority.js`). Rather than just claiming it, I'll check the live API with an independent script that recomputes each score from the raw fields using the spec formula and compares the order.

import json, math, sys, urllib.request
from datetime import datetime, timezone

BASE = "http://localhost:4000"
PREP = {m["id"]: m["prep_time_minutes"] for m in json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(f"{BASE}/menu-items"))["menu_items"]}
TYPE = {"dine_in": 30, "takeout": 20, "delivery": 10}

def ts(s): return datetime.fromisoformat(s.replace("Z", "+00:00")) if s else None

def score(o, now):
    waited = max(0, math.floor((now - ts(o["placed_at"])).total_seconds() / 60))
    prep = sum(PREP[i["menu_item_id"]] * i["quantity"] for i in o["items"])
    promised = 0
    if o["promised_at"]:
        mins = (ts(o["promised_at"]) - now).total_seconds() / 60
        promised = 25 if mins <= 30 else 15 if mins <= 60 else 0
    return TYPE[o["type"]] + (20 if o["is_vip"] else 0) + min(40, waited // 10 * 5) + promised + min(20, prep // 15 * 5)

def key(o):  # 5.1 score desc, 5.2 promised asc (null last), placed asc, id asc
    p = ts(o["promised_at"])
    return (-o["score"], p is None, p or datetime.max.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc), ts(o["placed_at"]), o["id"])

ok = True
for flt in ["", "?status=received", "?status=preparing"]:
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    orders = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(f"{BASE}/orders/queue{flt}"))["orders"]
    bad_scores = [(o["customer_name"], o["score"], score(o, now)) for o in orders if o["score"] != score(o, now)]
    ordered = orders == sorted(orders, key=key)
    statuses = sorted({o["status"] for o in orders})
    print(f"{flt or '(default)':20} {len(orders):2} orders  statuses={statuses}  scores_match={not bad_scores}  order_matches_5.2={ordered}")
    if bad_scores: print("   mismatched:", bad_scores)
    ok &= ordered and not bad_scores

print("\nDefault queue as returned by the API:")
now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
for o in json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(f"{BASE}/orders/queue"))["orders"]:
    print(f"  {o['score']:3}  {o['customer_name'][:16]:16} promised={(o['promised_at'] or 'null')[11:16]:5}  waiting={o['minutes_waiting']:3}m  vip={o['is_vip']!s:5}  id={o['id']}")
sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
EOF
